waypoints.name: Pinto Rock base (end of NF-77)
waypoints.note: Approach via NF-25 to Mosquito Meadows, then NF-28/NF-77 (rough road) to the base of the ~400' cliff, Gifford Pinchot National Forest.
waypoints.directions: From Randle, take SR-131 south and follow NF-25 about 19 miles into the Mosquito Meadows area, then turn onto NF-28 for 2.7 miles. Turn onto NF-77, a rough gravel road, and drive it slowly to the roadside pullout at the end, directly below the formation at about 4,700 feet. This is Gifford Pinchot National Forest, and the pullout sits at the base of the roughly 400-foot cliff.

waypoints.name: Pinto Rock summit
waypoints.note: 4-pitch regular route through a basalt band and chimney to the summit; descend via 2 raps (60m) or 1 double-rope rap off the north end of the east face.

rows.approach: From the NF-77 pullout, a well-used trail runs along the base of the formation. The West Face and North Side are different aspects of the same rock reached via short spurs off this main trail, generally under 15 minutes' walk from the parking pullout.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking lot on SR 20 just east of milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass. The trail follows Canyon Creek about 6 miles to the Mill Creek Trail junction, the start of this route's approach. The east-side line up the East Ridge starts elsewhere, at a locked gate on the Slate Creek road below Harts Pass (about 3,800 ft).

waypoints.name: Mill Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford Mill Creek just below the trail junction — last reliable, easy-to-reach water before the long climb toward Azurite.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Canyon Creek tread here and turn up the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail; maintained trail effectively ends beyond this point.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mill Creek Trail
waypoints.note: Tread disappears under heavy slide alder and downed timber left from the mine-era trail's disuse — expect a slow, scratchy alder-hacking bushwhack for several miles.

waypoints.name: Azurite Mine
waypoints.note: Flat ground amid the old defunct copper/silver mine workings on Mill Creek; the common overnight camp before pushing toward the Ballard basin.

waypoints.name: Azurite–Ballard basin
waypoints.note: Reached via roughly 3 more brush-choked miles above the mine; open basin at the base of Ballard's south slopes and a typical bivy before the summit push.

waypoints.name: South-face brush and gully route-finding
waypoints.note: Steep, loose terrain with several look-alike chutes low on the south face — picking the wrong gully here is the main way parties get cliffed out or turned back.

rows.approach: Standard approach: drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass and follow the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail (#755) up Canyon Creek then Mill Creek — about 11 miles (roughly 6 along Canyon Creek, then 5 up Mill Creek) to the site of the defunct Azurite Mine, then a further ~3 increasingly faint, brush-choked miles (slide alder and downed timber are common since the trail has seen little maintenance since the mine closed) to roughly the 14-mile mark, where a boot path continues about 1.5 more miles to Azurite Pass (6,680+ ft). A longer alternate, more often used for combined Azurite-Ballard trips, starts at the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (#480) near River Bend Campground: follow that trail ~8 miles to the PCT, then the PCT south ~1.5 miles to Horse Heaven Camp before joining the Mill Creek Trail to the pass — this option runs closer to 25 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of elevation gain.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: US-side approach, opposite the Depot Creek approach used for the West Ridge/Beckey route. Climbers take a water taxi (or boat, portaging Diablo Lake to Ross Lake) up Ross Lake ~15 miles to the Little Beaver landing/dock, then hike/bushwhack up the Perry Creek drainage to reach the base of Southeast Mox Peak's East Face.

waypoints.name: Southeast Mox Peak (Hard Mox) summit / East Face high point

rows.approach: Access starts on Ross Lake: from the Ross Dam trailhead on SR-20 (near milepost 134), hike the short Ross Dam Trail down to Ross Lake Resort, then take the resort's water taxi (or paddle a canoe) roughly 20+ miles up-lake to the Little Beaver Creek dock at the lake's north end. From the dock, follow the maintained (but lightly traveled) Little Beaver Trail west, paralleling Little Beaver Creek through cedar-fir forest with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, about 4.6-5 miles to Perry Creek Camp/Shelter, a three-sided log shelter that marks the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward the Mox massif. From Perry Creek Camp there is no trail: the standard line follows the Perry Creek drainage south, and staying in or right beside the creekbed itself gives the fastest travel (easy rock-hopping and scrambling) up to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the creek and forces climbers up onto a bank. The south (true left) side of the drainage is preferred here — it holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths, while the north side is a nearly impenetrable slide-alder thicket. Above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber where travel speed improves to roughly 2-3 mph, eventually gaining the upper Perry Creek/Mox basin cirque below the connecting ridge to Southeast Mox, with talus and (season-dependent) snowfields and moats guarding the final approach to the toe of the 2,400-2,500 ft East Face. This is a genuinely serious approach, not a formality: the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) spent a full two days and roughly 14 hours of actual travel time in the rain covering under two miles from the lake to the base, and described it as one of the worst approaches in the Cascades. Expect cold creek fords, soaked gear, torn-up skin from devil's club and slide alder (the plant the route is named for), and real route-finding judgment calls about which side of the drainage to commit to. Water is abundant the entire way (Little Beaver Creek, Perry Creek) but should be treated.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 134, down to Ross Lake and the water-taxi/trail network
